DXaUwJhjWoe.content: Denver's Missing Middle Housing Push: Zoning Reform in Action Comment "REPORT" if you want more Colorado housing policy updates like this! Denver is advancing major zoning reforms to address housing affordability. Key Highlights: Unlocking Housing Choices (UHC): Legalizes duplexes, fourplexes, rowhomes, and cottage clusters in single-family zones. 2026 Zoning Updates: Duplexes allowed on single-family lots, limits on oversized rebuilds, and affordable housing requirements for large redevelopments. Why It Matters: Targets "missing middle" households—too high for subsidies, too low for single-family ownership. Denver's zoning has long excluded mid-scale housing. State Pressure: Colorado laws now mandate ADUs, reduced parking, and housing action plans. Debates: Critics argue new duplexes may still be expensive, density doesn't guarantee affordability, and neighborhood character could change. Big Picture: Incremental upzoning shifts Denver from exclusionary zoning toward gentle density. Whether this truly improves affordability remains uncertain. And we're not alone. This month, HOME of VA released results of a new poll by a nonpartisan research firm. The findings confirm what we've been hearing on the ground in Richmond: • 91% say addressing housing affordability is a top or important priority — and want City Council to act. • 73% say there is not enough housing in Richmond. • 69% support spreading development citywide rather than concentrating construction in lower-income, traditionally Black neighborhoods — as we see today. DYVNstAGTri.content: Love Roanoke's walkable spaces? Sign the petition and tell our city council! Requiring single-family-lots-only was a 20th century innovation that has made our spaces expensive, it's made car ownership mandatory, it's made some school districts out of reach for those with less money, and it's made our public places unsafe to walk for kids, the elderly, and everyone else. Land-use reform, the freedom to have options other than McMansions, makes beautiful, liveable, human places possible. The reason villages and corner cafes don't exist in new neighborhoods, the reason kids can't walk to school and the park is that zoning laws in recent decades made it illegal to do what people had previously done freely - work to create spaces worth living in. After the reforms passed in 2024, some with the most time, money, and influence have worked hard to keep exclusionary zoning in place. They have the votes on council as of now. But before May 18, sign the petition to say that's not what everyone wants. Even better, join us May 18 to say it directly to city council. #roanokeva #strongtowns #zoningreform Petition: https://c.org/Jt7kDHHQjj

18115570264808850.content:
We appreciate the shares and signups!
In fairness, I suspect most people who want single-family-zoning-only are worried not about walkability, but rather they are worried about rapid densification (all-the-sudden high rise apts). These reforms actually help us AVOID rapid densification, because it allows for incremental development that increases with demand.
In fairness also in the opposite direction, one of the main backers of the lawsuit against the city (to fight for exclusionary zoning) has publicly criticized those wanting zoning reform by saying derogatory comments about us acting like Roanoke was supposed to be a place like Chicago “where you walk around.” So… those most in the know on all sides I believe understand that walkability requires density, which requires getting rid of restrictive zoning codes that ban all housing except single-family-lots.
The fear is the loss of investment, home values, and neighborhood change. The ironic piece is that walkable, human-scale density (villages, not Manhattans), is so desirable that those places make the land grow in value a ton.
